{"id": "39:6/q14", "question": "What does 'creation after creation' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the successive creations are fetal stages or a sequence beginning before the womb and extending beyond it.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q14/p1", "position": "Successive embryonic stages within the womb.", "reasons": "Early authorities list drop, clot, lump, bones, flesh, hair, and spirit with variants: Mujahid continues until complete formation; Suddi, Muqatil, Zajjaj, and Ibn Kathir add breathing the spirit; Qatada adds hair; Ibn Kathir adds sinews and veins. Tabari prefers this because the verse explicitly locates creation in the womb and cites 23:13; Razi cites 23:12–14; Baghawi 71:14; Study Quran prefers three gestational stages (23:13–14; 22:5). Ibn Ashur supplies ten stages from a five-millimeter nutfa and 33-day alaqa through fetal size, organs, hair, and circulation in month nine; Kuranyolu describes fertilization, implantation, muscles, vessels, and nerves. Sources differ in detail, not in locating the development in the womb."}, {"id": "39:6/q14/p2", "position": "Womb creation follows an earlier creation in Adam's back or fathers' loins.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, reported across commentaries, makes the womb stage follow Adam's back; Ibn Atiyya adds fathers' backs. Tabari rejects this for the womb-stage reading because of the verse's explicit location."}, {"id": "39:6/q14/p3", "position": "Creation spans the father's loins, the mother's womb, and life after birth.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi present this broader three-stage possibility."}, {"id": "39:6/q14/p4", "position": "Unity unfolds into multiplicity through names, qualities, and acts.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward reading situates staged creation through bodily, vegetative, and animal levels."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q15", "question": "What governs the accusative 'khalqan' and its following phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether the following phrase qualifies the verbal noun or the verb.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q15/p1", "position": "It is an absolute object of the creation verb, specifying successive kinds.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives خلقكم as governor; Samin identifies يخلق and says من بعد خلق can specify its kind or attach to the verb if خلقا only emphasizes. Ibn Ashur treats it as an absolute object specified by 'after creation.'"}, {"id": "39:6/q15/p2", "position": "'After creation' attaches to the verb while 'khalqan' supplies emphasis.", "reasons": "Samin sets out this alternative syntactic analysis."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q16", "question": "What are the three darknesses?", "turns_on": "Which three enclosing places, developmental states, or inward principles the phrase counts.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q16/p1", "position": "The mother's abdomen, womb, and placenta or fetal membrane.", "reasons": "This is the dominant transmitted set from Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada, Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Dahhak and others. Tabari describes nested layers; Dahhak calls the afterbirth السلى. Qurtubi calls it sounder; Ibn Ashur says the membrane protects the fetus and gives it an independent nutrient cycle. Kuranyolu specifies abdominal and uterine walls; Islahi a cavity enclosing the womb."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p2", "position": "The man's loins or father's back, the mother's abdomen, and her womb.", "reasons": "Majaz, Zajjaj, Mawardi, Tabarsi, Abu Ubayda via Ibn Jawzi and Qurtubi, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and Bursevi transmit this set. Tabataba'i argues a father's loins cannot fall within 'your mothers' wombs.'"}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p3", "position": "The father's back, mother's womb, and placenta.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this separate threefold set; Tabataba'i rejects a comparable loins–womb–placenta reading because of the explicit maternal location."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p4", "position": "The placenta, womb, and night.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this from Ibn Jubayr; Mawardi gives another night-associated reading involving placenta, inner parts, and belly, and Tabarsi also lists night among proposed darknesses."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p5", "position": "Sperm, clot, and lump.", "reasons": "Biqa'i relates this to emergence of sex when bones acquire flesh."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p6", "position": "The womb, membrane, and prenatal blindness.", "reasons": "Asad gives this set and cites 22:5 and 23:12–14 for recurring embryonic stages."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p7", "position": "The amnion, chorion, and decidua membranes.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu proposes three protective or nourishing fetal membranes."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p8", "position": "Bodily nature, vegetative soul, and animal soul.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward interpretation locates multiplicity within unity."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p9", "position": "Created nature, spirit's existence, and human nature; or body, nature, and self.", "reasons": "The Najmiyya interpretation transmitted by Bursevi varies its terms and compares physical birth with the seeker's second birth into the unseen heart and spirit; Hafez's caged soul and Tree of Tuba couplet illustrates departure."}, {"id": "39:6/q16/p10", "position": "Possibility, prime matter, and form.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this symbolic set."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q17", "question": "How does 'in three darknesses' attach syntactically?", "turns_on": "The grammatical governor of the second 'in' phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q17/p1", "position": "It modifies the creation verb.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it modifies 'He creates you.'"}, {"id": "39:6/q17/p2", "position": "It attaches to the preceding non-emphatic creation noun.", "reasons": "Samin argues the emphatic verbal noun cannot govern it and that the identical preposition already attached to the verb blocks another attachment; he reports Abu al-Baqa's rejected attachment to the emphatic noun."}, {"id": "39:6/q17/p3", "position": "It is an inclusion appositive of 'in your mothers' wombs.'", "reasons": "Samin permits repeating the preposition despite the intervening source phrase, since the material shares a governor."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q18", "question": "What do the hidden womb stages demonstrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q18/p1", "position": "God's power, knowledge, and skill reach concealed places.", "reasons": "Jishumi says instrument-dependent perception could not work in a womb; Razi refers to 3:6; Ibn Ashur, Islahi, and Kuranyolu say hidden development shows comprehensive power and knowledge. Nahhas says the darkness does not prevent sun or moon as it prevents creatures. Qushayri says the origin should prevent self-admiration."}, {"id": "39:6/q18/p2", "position": "The bodily stages invite love and remembrance of their giver.", "reasons": "Qushayri distinguishes organs bearing knowledge, power, and life from sense organs; souls and hearts love their benefactor and should remember God."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q19", "question": "What does 'that is God, your Lord' point back to?", "turns_on": "How far back the demonstrative gathers the proofs.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q19/p1", "position": "The Creator identified by the preceding acts.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur, and Tabataba'i connect the demonstrative to the creator and governor of humans, livestock, and developmental stages. Ibn Ashur says it summarizes proof, uses God's proper name for clarity, and invokes 13:16. Ibn Ashur says the demonstrative singles out that bearer of attributes, comparing 2:5."}, {"id": "39:6/q19/p2", "position": "All acts described since the surah's beginning identify Him.", "reasons": "Biqa'i extends the demonstrative to creation's preceding testimony, with all creatures attesting by speech or state; Ibn Ashur also relates the conclusion to the universe's creation and control."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q20", "question": "How is 'that is God, your Lord' parsed?", "turns_on": "Which nominative supplies the predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q20/p1", "position": "'That' is subject, 'God' predicate, and 'your Lord' adjective or apposition.", "reasons": "Samin gives this analysis."}, {"id": "39:6/q20/p2", "position": "'That' is subject, 'God' explanatory apposition, and 'your Lord' predicate or substitute.", "reasons": "Tabrisi gives this analysis; Samin allows the appositive and predicate arrangement."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q21", "question": "How is 'to Him belongs sovereignty' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is circumstantial, independent, or predicative.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q21/p1", "position": "It is an independent clause or another predicate.", "reasons": "Samin allows independence, a successive predicate, or a predicate after God and Lord; he also parses the preposition as predicate and 'sovereignty' as subject. Tabataba'i treats both following clauses as further predicates of 'that is God.'"}, {"id": "39:6/q21/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says sovereignty can be raised by the adverb in a circumstantial construction; alternatively it is a second predicate."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q22", "question": "What does God's exclusive lordship and sovereignty establish?", "turns_on": "The argument from creation and ownership to exclusive divinity, and its implications.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q22/p1", "position": "God alone owns, governs, provides, and deserves worship.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Qushayri, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Tabataba'i, and Islahi tie creation and provision to sole lordship. Tabataba'i argues pagans acknowledge one Creator but multiply lords, overlooking governance as part of creation; worship follows the managing lord through fear, hope, and gratitude. Bursevi says dominion has no partner in either life; Biqa'i says nurturer need not be sovereign, so the claim completes the proof."}, {"id": "39:6/q22/p2", "position": "Another god would either conflict with God or lack power, so divinity must be one.", "reasons": "Razi cites 21:22 and argues that rival power creates impossible conflict, while power

lessness is deficiency."}, {"id": "39:6/q22/p3", "position": "The Creator is beyond body, parts, and place.", "reasons": "Razi says the verse identifies God through wondrous acts, not organs, establishing transcendence."}, {"id": "39:6/q22/p4", "position": "God alone has real or absolute existence.", "reasons": "Qashani says other objects of worship have no independent existence; Bursevi describes essential unity and the true goal."}, {"id": "39:6/q22/p5", "position": "God has no need of human worship or benefit from it.", "reasons": "Razi reasons from necessary existence and self-sufficiency: eternal need would demand eternal creation, new need would be deficiency, and all the world's disbelief cannot harm the Creator. Nasafi says 39:7 clarifies God's independence."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q23", "question": "How is 'there is no deity but Him' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether it supplies a new predicate, an independent assertion, or a circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q23/p1", "position": "It is independent or a successive predicate.", "reasons": "Samin gives both possibilities; Tabataba'i says the two ensuing clauses predicate further of 'that is God.'"}, {"id": "39:6/q23/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial, expressing God's unique oneness.", "reasons": "Tabrisi permits this or another predicate."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q24", "question": "What does the final question ask or rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether the stress lies on the rebuke itself or the passive portrayal of diversion.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q24/p1", "position": "How can people turn from the only Creator and Lord to idols or other powerless objects of worship?", "reasons": "Tabari connects 10:32 and reports Suddi's address to polytheists; Zajjaj compares فأنى تؤفكون and Tabrisi 6:95. Qurtubi and many later commentators invoke the prior proof. Study Quran relates the false sons and daughters treated as intermediaries in 39:3 and the preceding realities in 39:5–6. Asad says literally 'how are you turned away' from truth; Durr cites 43:87."}, {"id": "39:6/q24/p2", "position": "Its passive form suggests people surrender to diversion despite innate reason and clear proof.", "reasons": "Biqa'i says their conduct is overpowered by pursuit of ruin despite nature and reason; Islahi explicitly describes yielding their reins to a devil."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q25", "question": "What is the grammatical force of 'how' in the final question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q25/p1", "position": "It is an adverbial or verbal-noun accusative meaning 'how.'", "reasons": "Tabrisi supplies the parsing."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q26", "question": "How does the verse relate to neighboring verses and other creation passages?", "turns_on": "Whether the link is to surrounding proof, the following judgment, or parallel gift passages.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q26/p1", "position": "It adds human and livestock creation to the surrounding proofs of divine oneness and governance.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats the human-creation clause as circumstantial or a renewed proof, comparing 7:189; Tabataba'i links both verses' creation and governance. Study Quran relates 39:5–6; Samarrai contrasts al-Nahl's order of human creation and livestock with this verse's first couple, descendants, and provisions. Asad directs readers to 4:1."}, {"id": "39:6/q26/p2", "position": "The next verse clarifies God's independence and individual judgment.", "reasons": "Nasafi cites 39:7 for God's independence; Islahi says each person returns for judgment and God knows every deed and secret."}, {"id": "39:6/q26/p3", "position": "The verse's gifts should move people toward gratitude and worship.", "reasons": "Asad contrasts the livestock of 6:143–144 with pre-Islamic taboos; Study Quran cites paired human beings in 16:72, 30:21, 35:11, 42:11, and 78:8. Qushayri frames God as Creator, Provider, guide, and teacher of unity and limits."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q27", "question": "How is the Qur'an's descent described in related reports on inzāl?", "turns_on": "The stages and timing of revelation in the broader material on descent.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q27/p1", "position": "It descended whole on the Night of Power, then gradually.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn Abbas report a whole descent to Gabriel or the House of Might followed by measured delivery; Ibn Abbas cites 2:185 and 97:1. Abu Shama explains رسلا and star settings. Ibn Kathir reports consensus on a whole descent to the House of Might. Ibn Hajar prefers this as sound, connecting Ramadan review to each year's revelation."}, {"id": "39:6/q27/p2", "position": "The needed annual portion descended each Night of Power.", "reasons": "Razi considers annual descent from the Preserved Tablet and remains undecided; Ibn Kathir attributes this possibility to Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and Halimi and Mawardi adopt it."}, {"id": "39:6/q27/p3", "position": "Revelation began on the Night of Power and continued piecemeal.", "reasons": "Sha'bi gives this third account."}, {"id": "39:6/q27/p4", "position": "Keepers transferred the whole Qur'an to Gabriel across twenty nights, and he delivered it across twenty years.", "reasons": "Mawardi's fourth account is called strange by Ibn Hajar; the ITQAN note records it as rejected."}, {"id": "39:6/q27/p5", "position": "The debt verse was the last Qur'anic verse connected with the Throne.", "reasons": "Ibn Shihab supplies this separate report concerning 2:282."}]}
{"id": "39:6/q28", "question": "What related terms and reports illuminate the call to turn toward God?", "turns_on": "The related lexical, ethical, and reported material's bearing on responding to divine gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q28/p1", "position": "Returning and gratitude answer divine benefaction; denial repays blessing with disbelief.", "reasons": "Jishumi defines ināba as returning, gives anāba/yunību, and contrasts denial with grateful recognition, glorification, and obedience. He defines takhwīl as a large granted gift; a hadith uses takhawwul for regular admonition, and Banū al-ʿĀṣ's khawlan means dependents or slaves."}, {"id": "39:6/q28/p2", "position": "Servitude means fidelity, following the Messenger, and sincere counsel.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits al-Kharraz's definition and argues worship is creation's purpose in 51:56; true knowledge arises through worship. A Muadh report begins with his request for an act leading to Paradise and away from Hell. Ali reports the Prophet never worshipped idols or drank wine."}, {"id": "39:6/q28/p3", "position": "Divine sovereignty gives hope of exalted stations and gifts.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits a Sufi saying that God's power to raise servants is reason not to despair."}, {"id": "39:6/q28/p4", "position": "Related passages with the lām suit movement toward creation's goal.", "reasons": "Samarrai's cited Durrat al-Tanzil notes other lām passages amid creation's beginning or land and sea blessings."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q01", "question": "How does the opening rhetorical question work?", "turns_on": "Whether the question's hamza precedes the conjunction or an elided clause.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q01/p1", "position": "Its missing predicate compares the opened, guided person with a hardened or sealed, unguided person; the ensuing woe supplies the answer.", "reasons": "The warning supplies the omitted counterpart; Zamakhshari and Razi compare 39:9, Samin cites 39:19 and 39:24, Biqai calls the mutual omissions hitbak, Ibn Kathir cites 6:122, and Ibn Ashur also allows the condemned person of 39:20."}, {"id": "39:22/q01/p2", "position": "The interrogative hamza precedes the conjunction, and the fa links the result to what precedes.", "reasons": "Zarkashi prefers this and argues an omitted verb fails in 43:18, 13:19 and 13:33. Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq call fa consequential; Bursevi allows man as relative or conditional."}, {"id": "39:22/q01/p3", "position": "The hamza governs an omitted clause or verb before the fa.", "reasons": "Zarkashi reports this alternative from Zamakhshari and rejects it in comparable examples; Alusi reconstructs 'are all people equal?' as the denied premise."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q02", "question": "Why is chest expansion contrasted with hard hearts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q02/p1", "position": "The contrast depicts full acceptance spreading through the believer's chest, whereas the heart harder than stone admits no remembrance.", "reasons": "Alusi prefers hardness over tightness since tightness allows some entry, names the heart because it governs the body, and contrasts the singular believer with plural rejecters to suggest believers' unity. Bursevi recalls light versus darkness and knowledge versus ignorance; Elmalılı renders the contrast."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q03", "question": "What does sharḥ literally mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is bodily or spiritual.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q03/p1", "position": "It means opening, spreading, or making spacious, originally of flesh.", "reasons": "Jishumi also notes explaining and cutting open; Bursevi and Alusi mention spreading meat; Qurtubi glosses spaciousness."}, {"id": "39:22/q03/p2", "position": "Here chest opening is figurative for spiritual faith and ease.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives sound reflection and belief. Ibn Ashur compares the relief of constricted breathing (26:13; 6:125). Bint al-Shati cites Moses' mission and five Meccan passages (20:25, 16:106, 6:125) against physical surgery; al-Raghib calls it light, calm, and spirit."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q04", "question": "What is God's expansion of the chest for Islam, and when does it occur?", "turns_on": "Whether expansion precedes or follows the acceptance of Islam.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q04/p1", "position": "God gives a person readiness to receive Islam, followed by acceptance and steadfastness.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies monotheism; Tabari adds knowledge of lordship, obedience and certainty. Ibn Abbas and Suddi describe establishment of

 Islam. Zamakhshari calls it لطف. Razi likens innate readiness to sulfur ignited by a small flame. Baydawi, Alusi and Bursevi describe original disposition and the chest as the heart's locus; Tabatabai adds discerning submission."}, {"id": "39:22/q04/p2", "position": "Islam brings joy and tranquility, so chest expansion follows its acceptance.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi contrast this timing with prior readiness and attribute it to Suddi. Ibn Ashur names confidence, resilience, freedom from doubt, wisdom, noble conduct, brotherhood, contentment, patience, hope and gratitude; the lam means for Islam's acceptance."}, {"id": "39:22/q04/p3", "position": "The verse describes prior readiness and the Prophetic report describes later expansion when light enters.", "reasons": "Alusi resolves the reversal in sequence by distinguishing earlier and later guidance, calling the answer wise redirection."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q05", "question": "By what means does God open and guide the heart?", "turns_on": "How divine action, proofs and human receptivity relate.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q05/p1", "position": "Divine proofs, graces and insight enable a receptive heart to accept and sustain faith.", "reasons": "Tabrisi gives strong proofs especially for scholars, continually renewed graces, and proofs resolving doubts and casting insights; he cites 47:17. Jishumi links prior proofs of unity and justice; Biqai describes responsiveness to evidence. Razi says readiness is needed for proofs and refers the predestination debate to 6:125."}, {"id": "39:22/q05/p2", "position": "God grants the fullest opening, while bad choices corrupt original receptivity.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes opening to divine wisdom and power and the opposite to changed disposition; Bursevi and Baydawi contrast God's gracious act with hardness attributed to the person."}, {"id": "39:22/q05/p3", "position": "God creates faith in the heart, and the description applies generally.", "reasons": "Qurtubi and Bursevi generalize to believers; Tabrisi includes all morally responsible people despite the address to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q06", "question": "Who is the person whose breast is opened?", "turns_on": "Named occasions differ, and other commentators take the description generally.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q06/p1", "position": "The opened people are Ali and Hamza.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Ata, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi pair them with Abu Lahab and his son or sons."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p2", "position": "The opened person is the Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Muqatil places Muhammad on guidance and Abu Jahl opposite; Kalbi and Muqatil are also cited for a revelation about him."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p3", "position": "The opened person is Ammar ibn Yasir.", "reasons": "Thumali and reports from Muqatil assign the revelation to Ammar."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p4", "position": "The description applies to every believer whose heart receives Islam.", "reasons": "Qurtubi and Bursevi generalize; Tabrisi says the Prophet's address includes all responsible people."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p5", "position": "The opened person is Umar ibn al-Khattab.", "reasons": "Naqqash reports the identification."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p6", "position": "The contrast concerns Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ubayy ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak transmits it from Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "39:22/q06/p7", "position": "The opened person is Ali alone.", "reasons": "Al-Qummi's tafsir gives this report, but Tabatabai objects that a single revelation of the whole sura conflicts with it."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q07", "question": "What is the light from the Lord?", "turns_on": "Whether light names guidance, Scripture, grace, decree or a distinct divine reality.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q07/p1", "position": "It is God's guidance, knowledge, clarity, insight, or certainty.", "reasons": "Suddi, Muqatil and many commentators gloss guidance; Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur compare light revealing truth to physical light. Ibn al-Saib and Ibn Ata say clarification, Ibn Abbas certainty, Tabatabai discernment, and Study Quran maʿrifah."}, {"id": "39:22/q07/p2", "position": "It is God's Book, followed and returned to.", "reasons": "Qatada names the Quran; Biqai describes the great clarification used in every matter; Jishumi links it to the prior verse."}, {"id": "39:22/q07/p3", "position": "It is divine لطف, favor and enabling grace.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari identifies لطف; Bursevi and Alusi describe illumination of signs in creation and revelation; Biqai stresses the benefactor Lord."}, {"id": "39:22/q07/p4", "position": "It is faith in divine decree.", "reasons": "Al-Qasim gives this inward gloss."}, {"id": "39:22/q07/p5", "position": "It may be a divine reality distinct from grace or enabling guidance.", "reasons": "Alusi offers this further sense by which truth is apprehended."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q08", "question": "What does the Prophetic report say about light entering the heart?", "turns_on": "How the report joins opening, light and conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q08/p1", "position": "Light entering the heart expands it; signs are turning to the eternal home, leaving worldly delusion, and preparing for death.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud, Qatada and Ibn Umar transmit versions. Ibn Umar calls the one most mindful and ready for death wisest. Tabatabai names transmissions through Ibn Mardawayh, Hakim Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir; Ibn al-Jawzi points to 6:125. Qurtubi explains good works, contentment, taqwa and care as outward signs, with Paradise as reward (32:17)."}, {"id": "39:22/q08/p2", "position": "The opening is divine light, calm and spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib connects Moses' prayer at 20:25 with this verse; Bursevi speaks of light, tranquility and spirit."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q09", "question": "Why is the believer 'upon' light 'from his Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q09/p1", "position": "'Upon' suggests settled, continuous guidance; 'from his Lord' identifies the full light's divine origin.", "reasons": "Alusi contrasts this with merely having light; Ibn Ashur compares 2:5, takes min as origin, and cites 24:35; Biqai stresses the benefactor Lord."}, {"id": "39:22/q09/p2", "position": "The believer is depicted as riding light and thereby discerning truth.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the unguided lack both spacious breast and light."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q10", "question": "What warning accompanies those favored with divine light?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q10/p1", "position": "People blessed with divine favors have enemies and should beware of them.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes the Prophetic warning."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q11", "question": "What is the grammatical role of 'for Islam' and 'he'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q11/p1", "position": "The lam marks purpose, namely acceptance of Islam; 'he' refers back to the person whose breast was opened.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur supplies both analyses."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q12", "question": "What does 'woe' mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q12/p1", "position": "It denotes severe punishment, misery and wretchedness.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives punishment; Ibn Ashur cites 2:79. Malik ibn Dinar calls a hard heart the worst punishment and links it to mercy being removed."}]}
{"id": "39:22/q13", "question": "Who are the hard-hearted people?", "turns_on": "Named opponents differ, while exposition also generalizes the condition.", "positions": [{"id": "39:22/q13/p1", "position": "They are any whose heart rejects admonition or faith.", "reasons": "Tabrisi describes habituated disbelief. Study Quran links wrongdoing and lost divine favor to sealing with many cited verses, including 2:7, 5:13 and 57:16. Qushayri includes the outwardly faithful who are inwardly veiled."}, {"id": "39:22/q13/p2", "position": "They are Abu Lahab and his son or sons.", "reasons": "Reports pair them with Ali and Hamza; Qurtubi includes Abu Lahab's children, and Abu Hayyan treats them as examples."}, {"id": "39:22/q13/p3", "position": "They are Abu Jahl and other unbelievers of Quraysh.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Abu Jahl; Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas extend to similar unbelievers; Thalabi and Mawardi give the wider group."}]}

{"id": "39:23/q04", "question": "Why is this discourse called the best?", "turns_on": "The grounds given for 'best': form, content, divine status, and effect.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q04/p1", "position": "Its expression is uniquely eloquent and inimitable.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Bursevī, and others cite eloquence, composition, genre, pleasing style and strong diction. {"id": "39:23/q13", "question": "What does mathānī mean here?", "turns_on": "The root's reference may be thematic recurrence, pairs, repeated recitation, mutual explanation, praise, or a named portion of the Quran.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q13/p1", "position": "Its accounts, judgments, commands, warnings and other teachings recur in varied forms.", "reasons": "Muqātil lists past peoples, prophets, Adam and Iblīs, Paradise and Hell, resurrection, plants, rain and Pharaoh; Ṭabarī cites repeated law and accounts; Zamakhsharī adds commands and prohibitions; Ibn Kathīr reports Ḍaḥḥāk's pedagogic purpose. Māwardī's report gives suras of roughly two hundred verses as another delimitation."}, {"id": "39:23/q13/p11", "position": "It means the succession of verses and suras.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports al-Kalbī's sequential account of mathānī."}, {"id": "39:23/q13/p12", "position": "Its repeated descent marks stages before and after inward annihilation.", "reasons": "Qāshānī reads the true Book as descending to the heart while it alternates between the Real and creation."}]}
{"id": "39:23/q14", "question": "Why does the Quran repeat material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q14/p1", "position": "Repetition makes admonition take root and reaches audiences who receive different passages.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī and Biqāʿī say resistant souls need repeated counsel; the Prophet repeated admonition three or seven times. {"id": "39:23/q15", "question": "What is the grammatical role of mathānī?", "turns_on": "How a plural form qualifies a singular Book and whether it is adjective, specification, or circumstantial.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q15/p1", "position": "It qualifies kitāban despite its plural form, because the Book contains many parts.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Naḥḥās call it an adjective and a diptote irregular plural; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes lack of tanwīn. {"id": "39:23/q16", "question": "How is mathānī read?", "turns_on": "Whether the yāʾ bears fatḥa or sukūn, and how the silent-yāʾ form is parsed.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q16/p1", "position": "The majority pronounce the final yāʾ with fatḥa.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report the common reading; al-Samīn allows adjectival, circumstantial, or specification syntax."}, {"id": "39:23/q16/p2", "position": "Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bishr pronounce a still yāʾ.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī attribute the reading; heaviness may prompt sukūn, with either an accusative or omitted-subject predicate analysis. {"id": "39:23/q17", "question": "What is the form and root of mathānī?", "turns_on": "The proposed derivation from doubling or return versus praise.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q17/p1", "position": "It is a plural connected with mathnā or muthannā, from doubling or turning back.", "reasons": "Jishumī derives repetition by adding a like; Zamakhsharī compares karratayn at 67:4 and paired forms; Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Suyūṭī, Bursevī and KURANYOLU give related forms; Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives mathniya, a turned-back thing."}, {"id": "39:23/q17/p2", "position": "It may derive from praise.", "reasons": "Bursevī relates it to muthnā ʿalayh; Ālūsī and al-Kashf examine the adjectival form."}]}
